data.name: Baseball Riot
data.detailed_description:
Baseball Riot is a fun physics based puzzle game packed with slapstick comedy and mayhem!



Take control of retired star batter Gabe Carpaccio as he goes on a crusade to free his former team from the grasp of Explodz Inc.

Smash baseballs at various Explodz fueled goons such as obnoxious fans, biased umpires, leery catchers and more. Bounce the ball of walls and platforms to knock out many targets with one hit.

Detonate Explodz crates to launch the baddies sky high! See the enemies tumble as hapless ragdolls and try to master each level by collecting three stars.

Conquer more than 100 levels and save the day!

FEATURES
  • Easy to learn physics based puzzle gameplay
  • Funny knockouts with ragdoll characters
  • More than 100 levels
  • Explosive chain reactions and destructible items

data.short_description: Start a baseball riot! Help Gabe Carpaccio take vengeance on the unholy alliance of his former team and a corrupt energy drink manufacturer Explodz Inc. in this fun physics based puzzle game! Baseball Riot is a sequel to Tennis in the Face.

reviews.review:
Baseball Riot is a lighthearted physics puzzle game that takes the familiar act of swinging a baseball bat and turns it into a series of increasingly elaborate trick-shot challenges. Rather than trying to simulate the sport itself, the game uses baseball as the foundation for environmental puzzles filled with ricochets, explosions, destructible objects, and cartoon slapstick. Developed and published by 10tons Ltd, it follows retired baseball star Gabe Carpaccio as he attempts to rescue his former teammates from the influence of the suspicious energy drink company Explodz Inc. The premise is deliberately absurd, but that playful tone suits the uncomplicated arcade experience extremely well.

Every level revolves around launching a limited number of baseballs toward enemies positioned around a compact environment. Directly hitting a target is easy enough, but the real challenge is figuring out how to eliminate several enemies with the same ball. Walls, floors, platforms, and other surfaces allow shots to rebound around the stage, turning seemingly straightforward situations into miniature exercises in geometry. Finding the correct angle can produce a satisfying sequence where one baseball ricochets through several targets before finally disappearing from the screen.

Environmental objects add another layer to the puzzles. Explosive crates can send nearby enemies flying, while destructible elements create opportunities for chain reactions and unconventional solutions. The exaggerated ragdoll physics make successful shots particularly amusing. Opponents are launched across the environment after being struck, reinforcing the game's comedic personality without making its violence feel serious. Obnoxious fans, biased umpires, catchers, and other unusual targets help maintain the deliberately ridiculous atmosphere.

There are more than 100 levels to complete, providing considerably more content than the simplicity of the mechanics might initially suggest. The stages gradually become more complicated as enemy placement and environmental obstacles demand increasingly precise shots. Completing a stage is only part of the challenge because players can pursue three-star results. This scoring system encourages experimentation and replaying earlier stages to discover more efficient solutions.

The controls are easy to understand, which makes the game approachable even for players who rarely play puzzle titles. Difficulty comes primarily from judging trajectories rather than memorizing complicated commands. However, the reliance on physics can occasionally become frustrating. A tiny adjustment to the aiming angle may completely alter a shot after several rebounds, and some stages can require repeated attempts before the correct trajectory becomes clear. At its best, this experimentation feels rewarding because an apparently impossible arrangement suddenly becomes manageable. At its weakest, it can feel like repeatedly making microscopic adjustments until the physics finally cooperate.

Players should also understand that this is not a traditional baseball game. There are no realistic matches, team rosters, seasons, pitching systems, or sports-management mechanics. Baseball is essentially the theme surrounding a projectile-based puzzle game. Anyone looking for an authentic representation of the sport will therefore find the experience extremely limited, while players interested in casual physics puzzles are much closer to the intended audience.

The visual presentation complements the gameplay with colorful 2D environments and cartoon characters. It prioritizes clarity over detail, making targets, obstacles, and interactive objects relatively easy to distinguish. The slapstick animation gives successful attacks personality, especially when an explosion sends several ragdoll characters tumbling simultaneously. The sound and presentation are similarly straightforward, creating an arcade atmosphere without distracting from the puzzles.

Its technical demands are extremely modest, making it suitable for low-powered computers as well as modern systems. The game also supports controllers, Steam achievements, trading cards, Steam Cloud, Remote Play on TV, and Family Sharing. These additions are not transformative, but they make the Steam release feel reasonably complete for such a small casual title.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable rather than Verified. The game runs successfully on SteamOS, its default graphics settings perform well, interface text is considered readable, and its functionality can be accessed through the default controller configuration. There are minor compatibility issues, including occasional non-Steam-Deck controller or keyboard icons, while some text entry may require manually opening the virtual keyboard. These inconveniences are relatively minor for this type of game, and its short puzzle stages are naturally well suited to portable play.

Repetition is ultimately the biggest limitation. Although new layouts, obstacles, explosions, and enemy arrangements create variety, the fundamental objective rarely changes. Players are continually calculating trajectories and trying to maximize the effectiveness of a limited number of baseballs. Those who become invested in earning three stars and discovering clever ricochets can get substantial enjoyment from the structure, while anyone expecting constant mechanical evolution may lose interest before completing every stage.

Overall, Baseball Riot is an entertaining example of how a very simple mechanic can support a surprisingly substantial casual puzzle game. Its accessible controls, more than 100 stages, amusing ragdoll physics, explosive chain reactions, and emphasis on creative rebounds make it particularly enjoyable in short sessions. Precision can occasionally become irritating and the formula eventually grows repetitive, but the satisfaction of executing a complicated multi-target ricochet remains strong. It is best approached not as a baseball simulation, but as a cheerful physics puzzler that happens to replace conventional projectiles with baseballs.

Rating: 7/10
